gaps.note: Commercial break edit hides the immediate reaction to the counter-offer.

stage_a.note: Smiling and enthusiastic delivery, asking who is ready to get their groove on.
Energetic gestures and engaged tone throughout the pitch.
Founders hug each other warmly and smile at the panel.

venture.description: A subscription service that prints up to 100 smartphone photos monthly into a bound, perforated book.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: The founders introduce their app that allows users to print 100 photos into a bound book for a monthly fee.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori receives a sample book and thanks the founders.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin asks what the charge is for the book.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states the monthly subscription price, which includes shipping and handling.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori compliments the price and asks what it costs them to manufacture the book.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian provides the exact cost to make each book.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori remarks that they have a very small profit margin.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms the exact profit margin they make per book.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks if they have generated any sales so far.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states their number of paid subscribers over the last eight months.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks them to calculate what they are making per month.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains they are not making money yet and specifies the number of customers needed to break even.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks why they are not currently making money.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian reveals their monthly overhead cost.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori asks who is manufacturing the books.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains they manufacture the books internally in their own print shop.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond asks if they have considered trying a different price point.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian says they want the book to be affordable for everyone in America.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond points out that nobody will get the book if the business closes.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie acknowledges Daymond's point.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark dismisses the broad vision and asks how much they have personally invested.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian reveals the dollar amount he has invested in the company.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert challenges the pricing model by asking if it would be the same without their existing print shop.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian says no, citing his proprietary software and specialized equipment as advantages.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert clarifies whether the cost would indeed be higher elsewhere.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms that the cost would be higher at another printer.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert points out the problem that the new business relies on the survival of the existing printing business.

turns.speaker: F2
turns.summary: Julie deflects by telling the story of how Brian developed the groove to make the book flexible for cheap shipping.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian demonstrates how the book flexes, allowing it to be mailed at a significantly lower postal rate.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark acknowledges that the groove is the core value proposition of their business.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks what the postage cost would be with standard binding.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian answers that the shipping cost would increase by three to four dollars.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark notes that any competitor would face an immediate four-dollar disadvantage in postage.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin asks if they would be willing to raise their price by a dollar.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms they would be open to raising the price.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark argues they are in the wrong business and should license the service to larger companies like Shutterfly.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian contrasts their low price with Shutterfly's much higher average book price.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark pitches his vision of licensing the technology as a service and makes an offer for those rights.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert states he cannot invest because the company is entirely dependent on their other commercial printing business.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond agrees with Robert about the structural risk with the printing partner and exits.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin asks if the founders would consider selling the entire company to him.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian replies that they would consider selling it at the right price.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin notes their initial valuation and asks again if they would sell the whole thing.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin makes an offer to buy the entire business outright for their stated valuation.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian says they would want to retain some upside rather than selling completely.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark clarifies his offer, emphasizing that they would keep the subscription business entirely.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert summarizes the two distinct offers currently on the table for the founders.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian counters Kevin's buyout offer by stating the company is worth significantly more.

turns.speaker: PANEL
turns.summary: The investors react with laughter and surprise to the high counter-valuation.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian repeats his counter-offer valuation of six million dollars for the entire company.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert reminds Brian that he initially valued the company much lower.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains the higher valuation is to account for the upside they want.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin refuses the high valuation but asks if there is a middle ground they can agree on.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states they want to keep at least half the company to have skin in the game.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert asks Brian what he thinks fifty percent of the company is worth.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian values half the company based on his original ask valuation.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Robert questions if Brian actually wants to sell half the company for that amount.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian explains he does not want to compete with Mark's proposed licensing model.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Lori offers to buy half the company to help them grow, and Robert joins her.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark asks Brian directly if he is willing to take Lori and Robert's deal.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian emphatically rejects the offer to sell fifty percent of the company.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Kevin announces he is joining Mark's licensing offer and revises the equity split.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark clarifies that his vision is for one-off purchases, not competing with their subscription.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond jokingly compares Mark's strategy to the movie There Will Be Blood.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Mark reiterates how the licensing deal would work for a one-time purchaser.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond summarizes the two distinct deals left on the table for the founders.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian states that they believe the licensing deal with Mark and Kevin is the better option.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Daymond asks if they are officially accepting the offer.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Brian confirms they accept Mark and Kevin's offer.

decisions.terms: $150,000 for 100% of the rights to license Groovebook as a service
decisions.note: Wants to license the proprietary groove to other photo apps.
Believes the business relies too heavily on their existing commercial printing business.
Agrees with Robert that the reliance on the printing business is too risky.
Wants to buy the entire company outright.
Wants to retain upside and counters with a much higher valuation.
Wants half the business, Robert joins her.

decisions.terms: $150k for 80% of the licensing rights, founders keep 20%
decisions.note: Kevin joins Mark's licensing offer and revises the equity split.
Accepts Mark and Kevin's licensing offer.
